title: Food Delivery System (Zomato / Swiggy)
description: Design a food delivery platform connecting customers, restaurants, and delivery agents. The order goes through a long state machine (placed → confirmed → prepared → picked up → delivered) and the system must dispatch agents intelligently. Multiple actors with asymmetric concerns.
prompt: Design a food delivery system like Zomato or Swiggy where customers order food from restaurants and delivery agents fulfill the orders.
prompt_note: This is a **multi-actor system**: customer, restaurant, delivery agent, and the platform orchestrating them. The biggest design temptation is to model 'Order' as one giant blob. Resist that — the order state machine is the central spine, and each actor interacts with it differently. Don't get lost in the menu/cart hierarchy; focus on the order lifecycle and agent assignment.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Three actors — customer, restaurant, delivery agent. All in scope?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Yes. Customer places orders, restaurant accepts/prepares, agent delivers."
clarifying_questions.why: Confirms the multi-actor scope. Each has distinct API needs.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "What's the order state machine? How does it transition through stages?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "PLACED → CONFIRMED (by restaurant) → PREPARING → READY → ASSIGNED (to agent) → PICKED_UP → DELIVERED. Cancellable until PICKED_UP."
clarifying_questions.why: Long, well-defined state machine. Each transition is triggered by a specific actor. Cancellation has a cutoff.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "How are delivery agents assigned to orders?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Auto-assign the nearest available agent when the restaurant marks the order READY. Use Haversine distance or similar."
clarifying_questions.why: Agent dispatch logic. **Strategy Pattern** for swappable algorithms (nearest, batch-with-other-orders, AI-based).

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Can agents accept or reject? Or is assignment forced?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "They can reject. If they do, find the next nearest. After 3 rejections, escalate."
clarifying_questions.why: Adds reassignment loop. Need to track rejected agents per order.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Payment — pre-paid or cash on delivery?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Pre-paid only. Assume payment processed at order placement."
clarifying_questions.why: Simplifies — payment is a precondition for the order, not a state in the lifecycle.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "How are notifications delivered to actors?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Via a NotificationService — assume push/SMS, don't implement."
clarifying_questions.why: **Observer Pattern**: state changes trigger notifications to relevant actors.

clarifying_questions.question: You: "Should we model the menu and cart, or just orders?"
clarifying_questions.answer: Interviewer: "Lightweight menu (item + price). Cart is just a list of items in an Order."
clarifying_questions.why: Don't get lost in menu CRUD. Focus on the order lifecycle.

core: **Customer:** browse restaurants, view menu, place order (with payment), track order status, cancel (until PICKED_UP).
**Restaurant:** receive orders, accept/reject, mark PREPARING → READY.
**Delivery agent:** receive assignment, accept/reject, mark PICKED_UP → DELIVERED.
**System:** auto-assign nearest available agent on READY. Reassign on agent rejection. Update status → notify actors via Observer.
**State machine enforcement:** invalid transitions throw (e.g., can't deliver before pickup).
out_of_scope: Payment processing, dynamic pricing, surge pricing, order batching, AI dispatch, multi-restaurant orders, ratings/reviews, search ranking.

core: **Atomic state transitions:** an order's status updates must be linearizable — no concurrent transitions to inconsistent states.
**Agent assignment is fast:** O(active agents) per assignment, distance-sorted.
**Notification on every state change:** decoupled via Observer so adding new notification channels doesn't change Order code.
out_of_scope: Sub-second latency, distributed agent location updates, geographic sharding, real-time map matching.

primary_scope: `placeOrder(customerId, restaurantId, items)` → create Order in PLACED → notify restaurant
`assignAgent(orderId)` → find nearest available → if agent rejects, try next → mark ASSIGNED
`agentDeliver(orderId, agentId)` → PICKED_UP → DELIVERED → free agent + release funds
`cancelOrder(orderId)` → only if not yet PICKED_UP → CANCELLED → refund
termination_points: `UnauthorizedActionException` — wrong actor (customer trying to mark PICKED_UP)
`ItemUnavailableException` — restaurant out of stock for an item
entity_intro: The system has three actors but **the order is the central entity** that all actors interact with. Treat the order's state machine as the spine; everything else (assignment, notification, payment) hangs off state transitions.

entities.name: Order
entities.role: **Model + State Machine.** The central entity. orderId, customerId, restaurantId, items, total, status, deliveryAgentId, timestamps. Status transitions enforced via `canTransitionTo()` map.

entities.name: Customer
entities.role: **Model.** Identity + delivery address. Just an ID + location for our scope.

entities.name: Restaurant
entities.role: **Model.** restaurantId, name, location, menu, status (OPEN/CLOSED). Owns its menu — items can be marked unavailable.

entities.name: MenuItem
entities.role: **Model.** itemId, name, price, available flag. Belongs to a Restaurant. Could be a record.

entities.name: DeliveryAgent
entities.role: **Model.** agentId, current GeoLocation, status (AVAILABLE/BUSY/OFFLINE). Location updated periodically (heartbeat). Status determines eligibility for new assignments.

entities.name: OrderService
entities.role: **Controller.** Orchestrates the order lifecycle. Validates state transitions. Triggers agent assignment, payment hold/release, notifications.

entities.name: DeliveryAgentService
entities.role: **Service.** Owns the agent registry. Provides `findNearestAvailable(location)` and status updates. Agents register themselves; the service handles assignment logic.

entities.name: DispatchStrategy
entities.role: **Strategy interface.** `selectAgent(orderLocation, availableAgents)` → DeliveryAgent. Implementations: NearestAgent, BatchedDelivery, ScoreBased. Allows swapping dispatch algorithms.

entities.name: NotificationService
entities.role: **Observer infrastructure.** Sends notifications to actors. Decoupled — Order doesn't know how notifications are delivered. Just an interface for now.

relationships.owns: orderId, customerId, restaurantId, items list, total, status, deliveryAgentId, timestamps
orders map, references to RestaurantService, AgentService, PaymentService, NotificationService

mvc_note: **MVC Mapping:** **Model** = Order, Restaurant, MenuItem, DeliveryAgent, GeoLocation, OrderStatus enum. **Service** = DeliveryAgentService (dispatch), DispatchStrategy implementations, NotificationService, PaymentService. **Controller** = OrderService (the public API for all actor interactions). The order state machine lives partly in `OrderStatus.canTransitionTo()` and partly in `OrderService.onStatusChange()` side effects.
schema_note: **Geospatial query** for nearest agent: store agent locations in Postgres with PostGIS, use `ST_DWithin` + `ORDER BY ST_Distance` for the dispatch query. Or use Redis GEO commands (`GEOADD`, `GEORADIUS`) for in-memory speed. For our LLD, we just iterate the agent map.

code_sections.label: Model — Enums + State Machine + Order
code_sections.flow: **`OrderStatus.canTransitionTo()`** is the heart of the state machine — a `Map<from, Set<to>>` enumerating all legal transitions. New states require updating just this map. **`Order.transitionTo()`** is `synchronized` and validates the transition before updating.
code_sections.edge_cases: Trying DELIVERED → PREPARING throws. Trying CANCELLED from any later-than-PICKED_UP state throws. The map is the source of truth — nothing outside the enum can fake a transition.

code_sections.label: Service — DeliveryAgent + DispatchStrategy
code_sections.flow: **`DeliveryAgent`** holds location and status with `volatile` for safe cross-thread reads. **`NearestAgentStrategy`** uses Haversine to compute distance, picks the minimum among available candidates.

code_sections.label: Controller — OrderService (the spine)
code_sections.flow: Each public method = one state transition triggered by one actor. After every transition, `onStatusChange()` runs side effects: notify, dispatch, refund, release agent. **The state machine validates transitions; the controller orchestrates side effects.**
code_sections.edge_cases: Customer cancels after PICKED_UP → `CannotCancelException`. Agent rejects an order → record rejection, retry dispatch. No agents available → escalate (notify operations team in production; throw here). Restaurant rejects order → CANCELLED + refund.

patterns.name: State Machine → OrderStatus.canTransitionTo()
patterns.why: The order has 8 states with strict transition rules. Encoding legal transitions in a `Map<from, Set<to>>` is **the single best way** to represent a state machine in Java. Adding a new state requires updating only the map — no scattered if-else logic. The validation lives in the enum, where it can't be bypassed.

patterns.name: Strategy Pattern → DispatchStrategy
patterns.why: Agent dispatch is a candidate for swapping. Today: nearest agent. Tomorrow: batch with other orders, score-based (rating + distance), AI-driven. Putting the algorithm behind an interface lets us A/B test or change without touching OrderService.

patterns.name: Observer Pattern → NotificationService
patterns.why: State changes must notify multiple actors (customer, restaurant, agent). The Order doesn't know how notifications are delivered (push, SMS, email) — it just calls `notify*()` methods. Adding a new channel = implementing the interface, no Order changes.

patterns.name: Saga (implicit) → Order Lifecycle
patterns.why: The order is a long-running multi-step process spanning multiple actors. If a step fails, you need compensating actions (refund, reassign). This is the **Saga Pattern** — though we don't formalize it. Production food delivery uses orchestrated sagas with explicit compensation handlers.
patterns.where: `OrderService` methods chain transitions + side effects with rollback (refund) on cancel

concurrency.issue: Concurrent state transitions on the same order
concurrency.fix: `Order.transitionTo()` is `synchronized`. Two threads attempting to transition the same order serialize. The state-machine validation happens inside the lock, so transitions are atomic check-and-set. **Side effects (notifications) happen outside the lock** to avoid holding it during slow I/O.

concurrency.issue: Two orders trying to assign the same agent
concurrency.fix: `DeliveryAgent.markBusy()` is `synchronized`. The first order's `markBusy()` succeeds; the second order's dispatch sees the agent as BUSY and skips it (not in the `findAgentForOrder` candidates). For finer control, the dispatch loop could retry with a fresh candidate list.

`currentLocation` is `volatile`. The dispatch may use a slightly stale location, but that's acceptable — it's a heuristic, not a guarantee. The agent updates every 5 seconds in practice; missing one tick doesn't change the assignment meaningfully.

Both operations call `transitionTo()` on the same Order, which is `synchronized`. If cancel wins, the order is CANCELLED — the agent's pickup attempt sees the new state and `transitionTo(PICKED_UP)` throws `InvalidStateTransitionException`. If pickup wins, cancel sees PICKED_UP and `cancelOrder()` throws `CannotCancelException`. **Either way, the system stays consistent.**

deep_dives.question: Why is the state machine encoded as a Map instead of a switch in transitionTo()?
deep_dives.answer: **Two reasons.** (1) **Single source of truth** — the entire transition graph is in one place, easy to read and audit. A switch scatters logic across cases. (2) **Open/Closed Principle** — adding a new state means adding entries to the map, not editing every method that transitions. Compare: 'where can I go from PICKED_UP?' is one map lookup vs. searching through code. The map approach also enables visualization (you could generate a state diagram from it).

deep_dives.question: How does agent assignment scale to thousands of agents?
deep_dives.answer: **Linear scan won't scale.** For thousands of agents, use a **geospatial index**: (1) Redis GEO commands (`GEORADIUS`) — O(N + log M) where M is total agents. (2) PostGIS with `ST_DWithin` and a GIST index. (3) Geohash buckets — partition agents into geographic cells, only scan agents in nearby cells. Production food delivery (Uber, DoorDash) uses S2 cells or H3 hexagons for hierarchical spatial indexing. **Mention the approach; don't implement** — it's HLD territory.

deep_dives.question: How would you handle the case where no agents are available for a long time?
deep_dives.answer: **Retry with backoff.** Schedule re-dispatch attempts at 30s, 1min, 2min intervals. After N attempts, escalate to operations (notify a human). On the customer side, show estimated wait or offer cancellation with full refund. In production: queue the order in a 'waiting for agent' state, periodically retry. Observability: alert when waiting orders exceed a threshold — likely a supply-demand imbalance in that area.

deep_dives.question: What happens if the agent's app crashes after pickup but before delivery?
deep_dives.answer: **Detection:** the agent sends location heartbeats every 5 seconds. If we stop receiving them for >2 minutes, mark the agent as OFFLINE. **Recovery:** the order is stuck in PICKED_UP. Operations team intervenes manually (call the agent, reassign if reachable, refund if not). **Better:** model an `AGENT_UNREACHABLE` state and trigger automatic escalation. This is one of those edge cases worth mentioning — production systems care a lot about it.

deep_dives.question: Why call notifications outside the synchronized block?
deep_dives.answer: **Don't hold locks during I/O.** Notifications might involve network calls (push gateway, SMS provider) that take 100ms+. Holding the order's lock during that time blocks all other transitions on the order. Pattern: do the synchronized state transition, release the lock, then call notify. If the notification fails, the state transition is still committed — we **prefer eventual notification consistency over blocking the system**.

deep_dives.question: How would you implement order batching (multiple deliveries by one agent)?
deep_dives.answer: **Extend DispatchStrategy.** A `BatchedDeliveryStrategy` would: (1) Look for nearby orders that need delivery from the same area, (2) Compute the optimal route (TSP — small instance, brute force is fine), (3) Assign all to one agent. The Order entity needs to support multiple parent assignments, or we introduce a `DeliveryBatch` entity that wraps multiple orders. Notifications get more complex (batch acceptance, per-stop status updates). **Significant scope expansion** — call it out as a follow-up.

deep_dives.question: How do you test this system?
deep_dives.answer: **Layered tests.** (1) **Unit tests on the state machine:** every legal and illegal transition. (2) **Unit tests on dispatch strategies:** mock agents at known locations, verify nearest is selected. (3) **Integration tests on OrderService:** mock RestaurantService, AgentService, PaymentService, NotificationService. Test full lifecycles: place → accept → ready → assign → pickup → deliver. (4) **Concurrency tests:** spawn multiple threads cancelling and progressing the same order, verify final state is consistent (no PICKED_UP + CANCELLED simultaneously). The dependency-injected services make all of this testable.
